The rye starter wakes slowly in a cold kitchen. Mine sat sulking on the windowsill for two days in February before it rose at all.

Feed it at night with warm water from the kettle, cooled until you can hold a finger in it. By morning the jar smells sour and grassy, like a field after rain. That smell is the signal. Bubbles alone can lie.

Mix the dough wetter than feels right. Rye holds water the way a sponge does, and a stiff dough bakes into a brick. Wet hands help. A bench scraper helps more.

The loaf wants a long, low bake. Give it a full hour at 200 degrees and let it rest a whole day before you cut it. The crumb sets as it cools, and a warm knife drags it into paste.

Before the oven door shuts, check the steam tray. An empty tray gives you a pale, cracked crust.
